question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in the recruitment process?
answer: For Bangladesh’s civil service, the key recruitment challenges identified in the assessment are the continued influence of personal and political connections despite the use of merit-based procedures; uneven application of those procedures across institutions and staff groups, with Class II–IV staff reporting less merit-based recruitment than Class I officers; and informal, word-of-mouth hiring channels associated with greater politicisation and nepotism. Job advertisements do not appear to reduce the relative importance of non-merit criteria. Written examinations and interviews can help reduce reliance on connections, but the assessment finds limited direct effects of these procedures on civil servants’ attitudes and behaviour.

In Bangladesh, merit recruitment procedures are widely applied in practice. 
However, the data suggests that there are important differences across institutions 
and groups of staff. Class I officers have more experience with merit recruitment 
procedures and less incidence of personal and political connections when entering 
the civil service compared to Class II, III and IV civil servants.  

However, personal and political connections do generally play a considerable role in 
recruitment and selection in Bangladesh and their effect on civil servants’ attitudes 
and behaviour has been shown to be negative.

Experience with merit recruitment procedures is associated with less politicised and 
less nepotistic recruitment. The Government of Bangladesh should hence consider 
the application of merit recruitment procedures across all classes of civil servants 
and ensure that informal channels of information and influence are contained during 
the recruitment process.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in managing the performance of the civil servants?
answer: The main challenges are uneven coverage and limited effectiveness of performance evaluations. Nearly 80% of Class IV officers had no evaluation in the previous two years, while nearly 90% of Class I officers had two or more. Performance outcomes are rarely discussed with superiors, and only a small proportion of civil servants receive feedback. Evaluations appear to have almost no effect on salary increases and only small overall effects on job satisfaction and other attitudes. They also do little to counter politicisation and nepotism in career advancement. These findings point to a need to review the system, while recognising that many officers in Classes I–III are evaluated regularly and believe ratings affect their career prospects.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in retaining the desired numbers and quality of the civil service personnel?
answer: Bangladesh’s civil service faces several related challenges in retaining the desired number and quality of personnel. About half of surveyed civil servants were dissatisfied with their salaries, regarding them as insufficient to support their families and uncompetitive with private-sector pay. Class I officers reported higher work motivation than lower classes but less commitment to staying in the public sector. Fears of politically motivated dismissal and involuntary transfer also undermine job satisfaction; reported threats of political dismissal reduce interpersonal trust. Career progression poses a further challenge: advancement depends substantially on seniority, transfers, and personal or political connections, while past performance plays a more limited role. Although performance evaluations influence promotion prospects, they are rarely linked to salary or dismissal decisions. Job satisfaction also varies markedly across institutions. Inferred implication: taken together, these conditions may make it harder to retain motivated personnel and sustain a merit-based civil service; the survey findings do not themselves establish how many employees leave for these reasons.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed at improving the retention of civil service personnel?
answer: The reform agenda most closely related to civil-service retention is the modernisation of pension administration, a pillar of Bangladesh’s PFM reforms. The PFM Reform Strategy 2016–2022 emphasises automating government business processes, while related work includes integrating payroll and personnel records and strengthening controls over payroll and pension payments. During the 2015 pay revision, linking payroll and pension databases to the National ID system helped remove “ghost pensioners”; that was a completed measure, not an ongoing proposal. Proposed priorities for pension administration are to establish a CPC, build a central processing, accounting and payment system, expand payment options, and clear the backlog of pension cases. The evidence identifies these as pension and PFM reforms, but does not establish a specific programme to retain serving civil servants or demonstrate an effect on retention.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed at improving the quality and efficient processes of the HRMIS ?
answer: The 2018 PEFA assessment identified three elements of Bangladesh’s HRMIS-related payroll reform agenda: continuing work on an employee database through a government-supported bridging programme after the earlier SPEMP-A effort stalled; considering technical assistance to link other cross-cutting issues with the payroll and pension database; and streamlining payroll processes using staff ID numbers. A 2023 PEFA assessment reported no specific ongoing payroll-control reform, so the available evidence does not establish that the 2018 measures remain active. It also noted that broader audit reform might lead to more payroll audits.

The Superior Direction and Advisory (DAS) System 

The military government in 1970 implemented the Superior Direction and Advisory (DAS) system, with little 
change to date. DAS offices are commonly referred to as cargos de confiança (offices of trust) and the 
appointees are regarded as recipients of the Minister’s or President’s personal trust along with being 
responsible for high-level decision making and advice (D’araújo, 2009). All the positions in the system are 
allotted by appointment and not based on set regulations or merit-based criteria.  

In practice, there are different levels of DAS offices, with distinct attributes. DAS from levels 1 to 3 are low-level 
positions, with little policy or managerial responsibility.

The offices directly responsible for high-level decision-making and advice are DAS-5, DAS-6, and Special 
Nature (NES) offices.

SOURCE: https://gov.br/gestao/pt-br/assuntos/gestao/outros/gestao-publica/arquivos-e-publicacoes/manual_orientacao_para_gestao_desempenho.pdf

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in managing the performance of the civil servants?
answer: Studies of Brazil’s public administration identify several challenges in managing civil servants’ performance: there is no single appraisal model suitable for every public body, so systems must be adapted to legal rules, organizational structures and political conditions. They also need clear performance standards, appropriate objective and subjective indicators, effective evaluator training, multiple sources of assessment, and feedback or performance-monitoring meetings. For the federal civil service specifically, research reports that the appraisal policy remains of limited effectiveness and has low acceptance among public servants; organizational culture, influenced by national culture and formal administrative structures, also strongly affects how performance management works.
quote:
SOURCE: https://bibliotecadigital.enap.gov.br/bitstream/1/7886/1/2023.09.30%20-%20Avaliando%20o%20desempenho%20do%20servidor%20p%C3%BAblico_EXTERNO.pdf
Identificou-se que não existe um modelo universal de AD aplicável a toda administração pública e que, em geral, as políticas de AD adotam um modelo baseado nas referências tradicionais da literatura, mesmo que não seja exclusivo ao setor público.

Os resultados apontam que é crucial adaptar abordagens tradicionais diante de aspectos contextuais impostos na implementação, como normas legais, estrutura organizacional e implicações políticas que influenciam a avaliação de desempenho e devem ser considerados no processo de implementação.

Como características das políticas, os resultados enfatizam a necessidade de padrões de desempenho claros e indicadores adequados, tanto objetivos quanto subjetivos, respaldados por treinamento eficaz de avaliadores. Além disso, identificou-se a adoção de múltiplas fontes de avaliação e a importância de reuniões de devolutiva ou de monitoramento do desempenho, mesmo que estas sejam informais.

answer: Cambodia is pursuing HRMIS modernization through a roadmap for a phased transition to a full-suite HRMIS. The roadmap envisages modules such as recruitment and performance management, with supporting change management, agile project management, and improved data analytics. An online payroll-data-entry prototype has demonstrated potential to improve HRM efficiency and quality at moderate cost. To address these challenges, the World Bank assisted Cambodia in developing a modernization roadmap for its HRMIS. This roadmap advocates a gradual approach to implementing a full-suite HRMIS, providing a sequenced and well-thought-out plan for the MCS to modernize their HRMIS through the phased development of key modules, such as Recruitment and Performance Management, in the short and long term. The roadmap also outlines key supporting measures to ensure these modules’ smooth development and institutionalization, including change management, agile project management, and improved data analytics. This approach aligns with Cambodia’s public administration reform and digital transformation goals.
Impact

A prototype for online payroll data entry service helped to demonstrate the potentials of digital technologies in improving HRM efficiency and quality at a moderate cost.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in implementing the desired compensation policy?
answer: Colombia’s public service faces six main challenges in implementing its desired compensation policy: (1) a dispersed salary structure with only small pay differences between adjacent grades; (2) too many grades—110 in the national executive branch—which hinder mobility; (3) different salary systems across entities, creating disparities and inequity; (4) limited scope for variable or results-based pay, with existing mechanisms failing to reward effort, individual or group performance, learning, and skills development; (5) comparatively low pay for senior public servants relative to other sectors, making recruitment and retention harder; and (6) the absence of a competency framework and weak links between performance appraisal, training, career development, and compensation.

Existen además diferentes sistemas salariales de acuerdo con ciertos tipos de entidades, lo que genera disparidad y condiciones de inequidad. An earlier, dated rollout plan for 2014–2016 called for updating employees’ CVs, asset-and-income declarations and institutional records; providing guidance, training and follow-up to 153 national institutions already in SIGEP; bringing in another 112 national institutions; and supporting information updates at 950 existing institutions and the entry of 1,200 new territorial institutions. These were historical plans and targets, not evidence that the targets remain current. A later implementation report documents migration from SIGEP I to SIGEP II: 48 district entities remained unable to migrate because their SIGEP I information was not up to date, so migration tests were under way with three of them. The tests also exposed an interoperability-standard issue affecting the transfer of CV information. The report identifies system-stabilisation and user-support work—including data-quality improvements, help-desk case management and incident resolution—as measures to help maintain coverage. question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed at improving the civil service recruitment process?
answer: Côte d’Ivoire is reforming civil-service recruitment by modernising administrative competitions and making them more accessible and transparent. Measures include greater use of digital tools, online registration and application submission through a single window, computer-assisted testing, and holding competitions in more locations outside Abidjan. Candidates can access free online preparation courses in place of in-person courses, while results are published in waves to shorten waiting times. Integrity measures include a ministry ethics committee, verification of successful candidates’ diplomas and online recruitment of personnel who help run competitions. Prefects are being involved in preparing, organising and supervising competitions, and competition cycles are evaluated to inform further changes. Workforce-needs programming is being strengthened through the Conférence de Programmation des Effectifs and coordination with ministerial HR directors. Specific competitions have also been opened to the Ivorian diaspora for qualifications that are scarce domestically, with examinations piloted in Paris in 2022.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in ensuring the desired level and quality of training in the civil service?
answer: The CAP 2020 evaluation identifies a weak continuing-training function across ministries and institutions. The main challenges are inadequate arrangements for planning, managing, monitoring and evaluating training, including a lack of tools, procedures and relevant skills; too few staff assigned to training; and weak follow-up after training, with very limited feedback, no lessons-learned sessions and no training reports. It also identifies insufficient initiative to improve internal programme management and limited engagement by ministerial cabinets, reflected in absent service-inspection reports and training files not being included in handovers.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed at improving the level and quality of training in the civil service?
answer: Côte d’Ivoire is reforming civil-service training through a new national framework for continuing training. The reforms include a procedures manual clarifying how training is managed and the responsibilities of those involved; a National Training Plan (PNF) to coordinate training, identify ministries’ needs and support planning and decisions on skills development; and the operationalisation of ministerial and interministerial training bodies provided for under Decree No. 95-92 of 1 February 1995. Ministries and institutions are also working to strengthen their training-management capacity, including within human-resources directorates, through better staffing, management tools and expertise in training design, management and evaluation. Other measures are the reorganisation of the National School of Administration (ENA) under Decree No. 2023-766 of 28 September 2023, with expanded initial and continuing training and diploma or certificate programmes; the development of professional placements, including placements abroad for diplomacy students; and digitalisation to enable e-learning and reach officials posted outside Abidjan.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in retaining the desired numbers and quality of the civil service personnel?

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in managing the performance of the civil servants?
answer: The key challenges identified in the Ghanaian Civil Service evidence are: (1) poor remuneration and low staff motivation, which the Office of the Head of the Civil Service links to low productivity, alongside widening pay disparities with other public-service organisations; (2) weak enforcement of administrative procedures and overlapping roles of Special Advisors or Special Assistants, which disrupt staff functions, workflow and accountability; (3) performance-management tools that have become routine and need review; (4) targets that are not sufficiently SMART, with some results dependent on budgets or stakeholder cooperation, making evaluation and sanctions difficult; and (5) a reported lack of linkage between public-service compensation and civil servants’ performance or productivity.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in retaining the desired numbers and quality of the civil service personnel?
answer: The principal retention challenge is uncompetitive conditions of service, especially low remuneration. The Office of the Head of the Civil Service reports that officers resign for better opportunities elsewhere, increasing attrition and causing a loss of valuable human capital; its 2022 graduate onboarding study also identified conditions of service as a critical factor in departures. Other reported challenges are inadequate office space and equipment, poor working conditions, and dissatisfaction with some roles and responsibilities, reflected in requests to change staff class. Poaching of skilled officers by NGOs and turnover after long-term training further deplete experienced staff. Limited resources for training, coaching, mentoring and succession planning, together with career-management and exit-interview weaknesses, make it harder to maintain the desired numbers and skills when officers leave.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in managing the performance of the civil servants?
answer: Kenya’s public service faces several connected performance-management challenges: performance contracts do not cover all arms of government; planning, resource allocation and results are poorly integrated; and institutional performance is not consistently linked to individual performance. The rewards-and-sanctions system is not fully operational, monitoring and evaluation are weak, and performance has limited influence on career advancement compared with seniority and qualifications. At the staff and management level, challenges include inadequate communication and understanding of performance-management and appraisal systems; limited participation in setting and owning targets; unclear job descriptions; difficulty setting SMART targets; inadequate appraisal skills; and weak work planning and alignment of targets with institutional strategic plans and Kenya Vision 2030. Limited managerial capacity to implement the system and inadequate identification of performance gaps and related skills-development needs further constrain its effectiveness.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in improving and maintaining the coverage of the HRM systems?
answer: The main challenges are fragmented and partly manual HR records, weak integration between HR and payroll systems, and limited system capacity. The public-sector HR database is decentralised rather than held by the Public Service Commission, and its largely manual records lack a sufficient audit trail. Kenya also lacks a fully digitised system that directly integrates personnel and payroll records, while linkages among GHRIS, IPPD and IFMIS remain limited. IPPD faces heavy monthly payroll-processing demands. The 2024 Payroll Management Policy further identifies stand-alone systems and limited interoperability, and reports that only three of GHRIS’s six modules were operational in ministries, departments and county governments. question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in ensuring the quality and efficient processes of the HRMIS?
answer: Kenya’s public-service HRMIS has faced fragmented employee records, manual HR processes (including leave administration), payroll delays, weak performance monitoring, and limited access to reliable HR information. These constraints have hindered efficient HR service delivery.
quote:
SOURCE: https://pefa.org/sites/default/files/2023-09/KE-May23-PFMPR%2BGRPFM%2BCRPFM-Public%20with%20PEFA%20Check.pdf
Public sector personnel and payroll management through the use of IPPD, IFMIS and GHRIS are good control activities but the major limitation is the absence of a direct linkage/integration among these software – potentially open an avenue for fraud and corrupt practices within central government payroll system. 

PI-23.3 Internal control of payroll 

The procedure for changes to personnel and payroll records is well established, clear and adequate to support the integrity of both personnel and payroll data. However, a fully digitised HR and payroll system which then allows for direct integration of personnel and payroll records is currently non-existent. There is also an opportunity for personnel and payroll data to be compromised due to the fact that the public sector HR database is decentralised and not residing with the Public Service Commission, a constitutional body specifically established for this purpose. Whereas the IPPD has an audit trail and passworded for access to authorised staff only, the HR database is largely manual, without sufficient audit trail.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed at improving the level and quality of training in the civil service?
answer: Laos’s 2015 Civil Servant Law sets out a framework for improving civil-service training. Training is to align with socioeconomic, human-resource and civil-service development strategies; incorporate new technology and improved foreign-language skills; and meet quality standards appropriate to its target groups. Civil-service management bodies are responsible for setting training and development strategies, plans, programmes and projects. These are requirements in the legal framework; the cited evidence does not establish which measures are currently being implemented as ongoing reforms.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in improving and maintaining the coverage of the HRM systems?
answer: The main challenge is the limited coverage of the Personnel Information Management System (PIMS). Although it is deployed in central ministries and agencies and provincial governments, it covers only about 50% of civil servants; district-level civil servants and teachers are the principal gaps. Coverage falls below 25% of the wider public-sector workforce because police, armed forces, and contractual and casual workers are outside the system. Limitations in PIMS’s functions and data architecture also prevent it from operating as a full HRMIS, hampering the government’s ability to manage civil servants and analyse and forecast the wage bill.

Les candidats externes à la haute fonction publique

Les candidats externes à la haute fonction publique 

De nombreuses hautes fonctions publiques tentent de diversifier leur vivier en recrutant des candidats 
externes. Selon l’Enquête de l’OCDE sur le leadership et les aptitudes de la fonction publique, l’attractivité 
de la haute fonction publique auprès de candidats externes passe, entre autres, par des campagnes de 
communication (21 pays sur 34), une recherche proactive des talents (12 pays sur 34) et des processus 
de recrutement dédiés (10 pays sur 34) (OCDE, 2020[6]). Cette recherche externe vise à développer un 
équilibre entre compétences et profils disponibles et non disponibles en interne.

La haute fonction publique marocaine n’attire pas suffisamment les candidats. En effet, l’absence de 
gestion de vivier ne permet pas de proposer un parcours de carrière aux candidats. Les conditions de 
nomination du décret n° 2.12.412 du 11 octobre 2012 poussent les hauts fonctionnaires à quitter leur poste 
après 10 ans de service maximum. Cette limite temporelle peut être bénéfique, mais elle doit 
s’accompagner d’une politique de capitalisation de l’expérience des fonctionnaires sortants. 
[EN: External candidates for the senior civil service. External candidates for the senior civil service. Many senior civil services try to diversify their candidate pools by recruiting external candidates. According to the OECD Survey on Public Service Leadership and Capability, attracting external candidates to the senior civil service involves, among other things, communication campaigns (21 of 34 countries), proactive talent searches (12 of 34 countries), and dedicated recruitment processes (10 of 34 countries) (OECD, 2020[6]). This external search aims to balance skills and profiles available internally with those not available internally. Morocco’s senior civil service does not attract enough candidates. The absence of talent-pool management means it cannot offer candidates a career path. The appointment conditions in Decree No. 2.12.412 of 11 October 2012 lead senior civil servants to leave their posts after a maximum of 10 years’ service. This time limit can be beneficial, but it should be accompanied by a policy for making use of departing civil servants’ experience.]

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in managing the performance of the civil servants?
answer: The key challenges are that performance appraisal remains underused despite its formal role, while career advancement depends more on qualifications and seniority than on assessed performance. Appraisals commonly use a 20-point scale on which any score below 20 is perceived as a sanction, discouraging managers from giving honest and fair feedback. For senior civil servants, ministries manage their own officials and assessment criteria vary across administrations. Reviews have limited consequences for career progression: dismissal for poor performance is rarely applied, and strong performance is not consistently linked to training support or financial rewards.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed to improve the performance management of the civil servants?
answer: Morocco is progressively moving from a career-based civil-service model toward one based on competencies, with changes to the legal and regulatory framework under development. For performance management specifically, the Court of Accounts recommends overhauling appraisal and promotion: each administration would define evaluation criteria tied to employees’ assigned tasks; advancement and promotion would become less automatic and give greater weight to performance, initiative, innovation and skills development; and the system would provide for consequences for poor performance and recognition of exceptional performance. These appraisal measures are recommendations, not evidence that they have been implemented across the civil service.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed at improving the civil service recruitment process?
answer: Mozambique’s 2022 civil-service framework assigns the central SNGRHE governing body responsibility for developing recruitment and selection policies, defining implementation rules and procedures, and monitoring and controlling recruitment and selection activities across the state apparatus. Sectoral bodies are responsible for planning, carrying out and improving recruitment, selection and staff assignment in their respective sectors, under the central body’s policies and plans.
quote:
SOURCE: https://cmnampula.gov.mz/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/mz-government-gazette-series-i-dated-2022-06-17-no-116.pdf
Article 28 (Competences of the Central Governing Body)

The Central Governing Body of the SNGRHE is the entity responsible for the public-service area.

In recruitment and selection, it is responsible for:
a) conducting studies and research aimed at establishing recruitment and selection policies for human resources in the State apparatus and defining norms and procedures for their implementation;
b) monitoring, guiding and controlling the implementation of recruitment and selection activities for human resources in the State apparatus, systematically evaluating them to ensure correct application of the General Statute of State Employees and Agents.

Article 29 (Competences of Sectoral Bodies)

In recruitment and selection, sectoral bodies are responsible for:
a) planning, programming and carrying out recruitment, selection and staff-assignment activities, based on policies and plans defined for the sector;
b) conducting studies and research on recruitment and selection for their continuous improvement; and
c) promoting, coordinating, guiding, evaluating and controlling recruitment and selection processes in their sector.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in implementing the desired compensation policy?
answer: Key challenges include containing compensation costs while making pay more effective. Mozambique’s single salary scale (TSU) simplified payroll and promoted pay equity, but increased salaries by 13.6% without translating into stronger incentives for improved service delivery. The public-sector wage bill reached 14% of GDP in 2024. Persistent geographic imbalances in staffing, wage drift caused by policy distortions, and a progression structure that can lead to rapid and costly promotions further complicate efforts to keep compensation sustainable while supporting service delivery.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in retaining the desired numbers and quality of the civil service personnel?
answer: In Mozambique, a directly documented retention challenge is that HR and remuneration policies have been designed in isolation rather than as a coherent package. The seniority allowance was originally targeted at experienced staff with scarce, sought-after skills, such as doctors, to encourage them to stay in public service. Extending it to all civil servants reduced its average value and weakened its role as an incentive to retain key personnel. The assessment also reports that available funding affects whether authorized posts are filled and that the government lacks a centralized, aggregated workforce plan. These are challenges to maintaining the desired number and mix of staff; their effect on retention across the civil service is an inference, not a directly established finding.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed at improving the retention of civil service personnel?

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed at improving and maintaining the coverage of the HRM systems?
answer: Mozambique’s HRM-system coverage reforms focus on extending and strengthening e-SNGRHE. A 2020 government progress report recorded preparations to deploy it in the Ministries of National Defence and Mineral Resources and Energy, and work to integrate municipalities, particularly Matola and Maputo City. A 2025 World Bank assessment reports that e-SNGRHE covers about 96% of public employees nationwide. To improve and maintain effective coverage, it recommends modernising the system and its data-analysis functions, progressively digitising HRM processes and improving data quality, and supporting interoperability with e-SISTAFE. These are recommendations, not evidence that every upgrade is already being implemented. An earlier, separate 2018 action plan also called for an integrated HR information system and nationwide completion of e-folha rollout in local government bodies; it does not establish that those actions remain ongoing.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in ensuring the quality and efficient processes of the HRMIS?
answer: Despite the e-SNGRHE’s broad coverage, HR processes and approvals remain largely paper-based, so digitalisation has not delivered an efficient end-to-end process. HR focal points—the only authorised users—must enter information manually, which is time-consuming and prone to error. Supporting documents cannot be uploaded, making it impossible to audit the accuracy of all information entered. Weak data-analysis functions and unavailable historical employee data also prevent the system from adequately supporting workforce planning and career management.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed at improving the quality and efficient processes of the HRMIS ?
answer: Mozambique’s documented HRMIS reforms centred on the National State Human Resources Management System (SNGRHE), designed to record and track the employment cycle of civil servants and state agents and improve payroll control. A 2020 progress report said five modules had been developed—for personnel administration, careers and remuneration, performance appraisal, establishment planning, and recruitment and selection—and that the first three were being piloted in 17 institutions, including eight at central level. Related process reforms included updating e-CAF salary-calculation rules for transfers, career changes, promotions and progression; validating the transfer of administrative acts from SNGRHE to e-CAF so they could be managed through SNGRHE; and updating payroll workflows to control loading and exclusion of payrolls subject to an exception calendar. A 2018 action plan also called for an integrated HR information system and completion of e-folha implementation in local bodies. These are reforms documented in plans and progress reporting, not confirmation that every measure remains underway today. A later World Bank assessment recommends better HR-data quality, staff-presence monitoring and payroll forecasting, but those recommendations should not be treated as confirmed ongoing reforms.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed to improve the performance management of the civil servants?
answer: Nigeria’s federal civil-service reform replaces the Annual Performance Evaluation Report (APER) with a Performance Management System (PMS) for Federal Ministries, Extra-Ministerial Departments and Agencies. The PMS is intended to set employee goals and objectives, track, assess and report individual performance, and emphasize measurable performance objectives, targets and relevant competencies. It also provides for results-oriented performance management and training, with annual individual goals following the finalisation of MDA institutional and departmental goals and targets.

question: What were the latest major changes to the laws and regulations governing civil service functioning in the country and when did they take place?
answer:
The latest changes identified in the retrieved evidence concern Romania’s Administrative Code, Government Emergency Ordinance (OUG) No. 57/2019. In chronological order:

1. **2020 — OUG No. 164/2020:** Allowed management civil-service posts to be filled temporarily without a competition during a state of siege, emergency or alert, and for up to 60 days afterward, subject to prior notification of the National Agency of Civil Servants (ANFP).
2. **2021 — OUG No. 4/2021, OUG No. 138/2021 and Law No. 153/2021:** The prefect and subprefect posts became public-dignity offices, and the senior civil-service post of secretary-general of the prefect’s institution was created. Rules were added for equating certain specific and general civil-service posts; deadlines for a pilot recruitment project and the effective date of specified recruitment provisions were deferred. Annex 7 established rules for disciplinary commissions and procedures.
3. **2022–2023 — OUG No. 191/2022 and Law No. 348/2023:** The 2022 ordinance amended and supplemented the Administrative Code and was approved with amendments and additions by the 2023 law.
4. **2023 — OUG No. 121/2023:** Further amended and supplemented the Code, including provisions concerning recruitment to civil-service posts.
5. **February 2026 — OUG No. 7/2026:** The latest amendment identified in the retrieved material added transitional provisions to OUG No. 191/2022 concerning deadlines and rules for evaluating senior, management and executive civil servants’ performance for work performed in 2025 and 2026. This was a targeted transitional change, rather than a replacement of the Administrative Code.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed at improving the level and quality of training in the civil service?
answer: Romania is expanding and reshaping civil-service training through several connected reforms. Under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR), a digital-skills programme provides advanced training for civil servants and leadership and talent-management training for managers in the context of digital transformation. ANFP reported that 27,579 civil servants had been trained and certified by 31 July 2025: 25,039 in advanced digital skills and 2,540 managers in leadership and talent management. Alongside this, PNRR public-sector human-resources reforms are introducing competency frameworks to guide staff development. Project 24RO12 is developing a general digital-competency framework for civil servants through ANFP, the Digitalisation Authority and the National Institute of Administration, with World Bank support. Project 25RO58 is designing and piloting learning packages for HR personnel, managers and digital-transformation leaders, covering areas such as competency-based workforce planning, analytical and digital HR skills, performance management and strategic HR management. Separately from those activities already under way, ANFP recommends replacing fragmented, episodic courses with continuous professional learning. Its proposed model includes a digital academy, a minimum annual training portfolio tailored to job type and competency requirements, modules in ethics, digitalisation, cybersecurity, data protection, public policy and service management, stronger links between training, appraisal and promotion, and recognition of formal and non-formal learning.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in improving and maintaining the transparency of the HRMIS systems?

Inferred implication for transparency: these gaps make it harder to maintain a consistent, reliable view of public-sector HR information.

answer: Senegal’s identified compensation-policy reform was to prepare a plan to harmonise public-sector remuneration, one of the National Administration Forum’s eight priority measures. question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed at improving the level and quality of training in the civil service?
answer: Senegal’s central reform is the National Strategy for Continuing Training of State Agents. It aims to improve the quality and relevance of training by renovating its financing and aligning training offered by technical and financial partners with national priorities. Implementation is intended to strengthen cooperation among the ministry responsible for the public service, sector ministries, state agents, training providers and partners. The authorities also plan to adapt the legislative and regulatory framework so that every public agent, from senior managers to operational staff, receives training at least once a year. Training is intended to continue throughout an agent’s career and cover both occupation-specific skills and cross-cutting subjects.

Respondents identified several performance-management challenges: too little praise and feedback, including limited feedback from the government; differing views on how to use sanctions and rewards; difficulty reassigning or removing unsuitable agency heads, including where cooperation had broken down; and concerns that pay was not sufficiently competitive. They also pointed to the need for opportunities to move into new, stimulating assignments. These are respondents’ views in a 2003 report, not a current assessment of challenges across Sweden’s civil service.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed to improve the performance management of the civil servants?
answer: The available evidence identifies two ongoing initiatives relevant to performance in Sweden’s public administration, but neither is documented as a reform of individual civil-servant appraisals. The continuing trust-based governance reform (Tillitsreformen) aims to streamline administration and develop government agencies’ internal governance. Separately, Statskontoret is working to improve evaluation practices; an OECD assessment notes that Sweden still lacks a comprehensive system for monitoring the results of all aspects of its strategic framework. Inference: these initiatives may improve how agencies manage and assess performance, but the evidence does not establish a specific new performance-management system for civil servants.

question: What are the key challenges that your service has been facing in the recruitment process?
answer: The key recruitment challenges are limited perceived meritocracy and persistent nepotism; recruitment often prioritises degrees over practical skills; candidate assessment does not comprehensively or systematically evaluate skills and competencies; recruitment standards are not applied consistently; and ministries and agencies need stronger capacity to manage recruitment effectively.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed to improve the civil service compensation policy?
answer: Uzbekistan’s ongoing reform aims to establish a unified civil-service remuneration system that links pay to performance, qualifications and position category. Under the Civil Service Development Strategy to 2030, the government tasked the Ministry of Economy and Finance, the Ministry of Employment and Poverty Reduction, and the Civil Service Development Agency with submitting a draft presidential decree by 1 November 2025. The proposed change would determine official salaries from 1 January 2026 under a common principle that considers work experience, academic and qualification levels, performance and other indicators. Earlier reform measures also sought to eliminate pay differences between ministries and agencies and link material incentives to key performance indicators, professional competencies, and the complexity and responsibility of duties. Separately, the World Bank has recommended a common grading and salary framework and incorporating bonuses and allowances into base pay; these are recommendations, not established elements of the planned decree.

question: What are the ongoing reforms aimed to improve the performance management of the civil servants?
answer: Uzbekistan’s ongoing reform aims to make civil servants’ performance assessments more consistent and competency-based. A forthcoming competency framework is intended to underpin assessments, while ARGOS is to develop evaluation criteria and procedures aligned with it. ARGOS had drafted several regulatory acts on performance evaluation, but they had not been adopted as of the OECD’s 2024 review; a standardised assessment process therefore remained a reform objective, not an established system. Separately, the 2022 civil service law provides for evaluation against key performance indicators (KPIs), with the methodology set by a specially authorised state body and internal procedures determined by each state body.
